title: Polar and exponential form of complex numbers

items.title: Forms of Complex Numbers (Rectangular, Polar, Euler)

moments.title: Three forms of a complex number
moments.text: The video introduces Cartesian, polar and exponential representations.

moments.title: Plot a Cartesian number
moments.text: For $z=1+\sqrt3\,i$, plot the point $(1,\sqrt3)$ on the complex plane.

moments.title: Modulus and argument
moments.text: Polar form uses the distance from the origin and an angle measured from the positive real axis.

moments.title: Find the modulus
moments.text: Using the right triangle, $|z|=\sqrt{1^2+(\sqrt3)^2}=2$.

moments.title: Find the argument
moments.text: The first-quadrant example has $\arg z=\pi/3$ radians.

moments.title: What cis means
moments.text: $\operatorname{cis}\theta$ is shorthand for $\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

moments.title: Write polar form
moments.text: Using modulus 2 and argument $\pi/3$, the example becomes $2\operatorname{cis}(\pi/3)$.

moments.title: Write exponential form
moments.text: The same complex number is $2e^{i\pi/3}$.

moments.title: Choose a useful form
moments.text: The presenter compares Cartesian form for addition and subtraction with polar or exponential form for products, quotients and powers.

moments.title: Relate Cartesian and polar forms
moments.text: The video moves to a geometric explanation of the polar expression.

moments.title: Resolve the vector
moments.text: For the first-quadrant diagram, $a=r\cos\theta$ and $b=r\sin\theta$.

moments.title: Factor out the modulus
moments.text: Substitution into $a+bi$ gives $r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, written $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$.

notes.title: Positive and negative arguments
notes.text: The video describes an argument as measured counterclockwise. A clockwise angle can also represent an argument, and principal arguments are often negative in the lower half-plane.
notes.write: Use the convention requested. For example, $-\pi/4$ and $7\pi/4$ describe the same direction.

moments.title: Operations and representations
moments.text: The video compares addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and powers in Cartesian, polar and exponential forms.

moments.title: Addition and subtraction
moments.text: In Cartesian form, add or subtract real parts and imaginary parts separately.

moments.title: Add two complex numbers
moments.text: The presenter adds $1+\sqrt3\,i$ and $2+2i$, obtaining $3+(2+\sqrt3)i$.

moments.title: Multiplication and division
moments.text: The video explains that several forms can be used, then starts with Cartesian multiplication.

moments.title: Expand the product
moments.text: Multiply the binomials and replace $i^2$ by $-1$, then collect real and imaginary parts.

moments.title: Polar multiplication
moments.text: For nonzero complex numbers in polar form, multiply moduli and add arguments.

moments.title: Divide in Cartesian form
moments.text: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the nonzero denominator to obtain a real denominator.

moments.title: Polar and exponential division
moments.text: Divide moduli and subtract arguments; the denominator must be nonzero.

moments.title: Powers
moments.text: The presenter compares repeated Cartesian multiplication with raising the modulus and multiplying the argument in polar form.

moments.title: Raise to the fourth power
moments.text: For $z=2\operatorname{cis}(\pi/3)$, the fourth power is $16\operatorname{cis}(4\pi/3)$.

moments.title: A remark about roots
moments.text: The presenter briefly mentions roots at the end; solving for all complex roots requires accounting for all arguments.

notes.title: Finding all complex roots
notes.text: The closing remark suggests that roots work exactly like taking a fractional power. A complex equation can have multiple roots, so one calculator value is not necessarily the complete solution.
notes.write: When solving $z^n=w$, account for all distinct arguments. Complex roots are not required in the syllabus guidance for AHL 1.13.

moments.title: Calculator settings and operations
moments.text: The video introduces complex-number settings, input, stored values and conversion tools on a TI-Nspire.

moments.title: Choose the output format
moments.text: The presenter contrasts real, rectangular and polar output settings.

moments.title: A non-real calculation
moments.text: The presenter demonstrates why a real-only setting can reject an expression involving $\sqrt{-1}$.

moments.title: Switch to polar output
moments.text: The video shows how the TI-Nspire can display an entered Cartesian number in polar or exponential form.

moments.title: Enter Cartesian, polar and exponential forms
moments.text: The presenter demonstrates input conventions for the three forms.

moments.title: Store a complex number
moments.text: A stored variable can be reused for later calculations and operations.

moments.title: Return to rectangular output
moments.text: The stored value is displayed in rectangular form; the video discusses decimal output.

moments.title: Conversion tools
moments.text: The presenter locates tools for conjugates, components, angle, magnitude and conversions between forms.

moments.title: Keep hand methods and exact forms
moments.text: The presenter recommends remaining proficient with exact algebra as well as calculator approximations.

notes.title: Calculator shown
notes.text: The video uses a TI-Nspire, so its key presses and output behaviour should not be assumed to match the Casio fx-CG50.
notes.write: Check the Casio complex-number and angle settings, and use the output form requested by the question.

ican.text: I can convert between Cartesian, modulus-argument and exponential forms, using a specified argument convention.
I can find the modulus and argument from an Argand diagram and check the correct quadrant.
I can multiply and divide nonzero complex numbers in polar or exponential form and calculate integer powers.
I can interpret multiplication as a rotation and scaling in the complex plane.
I can combine sinusoidal functions with the same frequency into a single sinusoidal expression.
I can use technology to check forms and calculations while preserving exact values when required.

ku.text: For $z=a+bi\ne0$, the modulus is $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and an argument $\theta$ satisfies $a=r\cos\theta$, $b=r\sin\theta$.
Polar form is $r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)=r\operatorname{cis}\theta$; exponential form is $re^{i\theta}$. Arguments that differ by $2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, represent the same direction.
For $z\ne0$, use its quadrant and the requested interval to select an argument. The number zero has modulus 0 and no defined argument.
For $z_1=r_1e^{i\theta_1}$ and $z_2=r_2e^{i\theta_2}$ with nonzero $z_2$, multiplication gives $r_1r_2e^{i(\theta_1+\theta_2)}$ and division gives $(r_1/r_2)e^{i(\theta_1-\theta_2)}$.
For an integer $n$, $z^n=r^ne^{in\theta}$ where the expression is defined. Adjust the final angle to the requested principal-argument interval if needed.
Multiplication by $re^{i\theta}$ scales distances from the origin by $r$ and rotates arguments by $\theta$.

Sinusoids of the same frequency can be combined by adding their complex coefficients, or by expanding and collecting cosine and sine terms. The amplitude and phase of the result come from the resulting coefficients.

misc.better: $-1+i$ is in quadrant II, so its principal argument is $3\pi/4$.

misc.weak: When multiplying complex numbers in polar form, add the moduli.

misc.better: Raise the modulus to the fourth power and multiply the argument by 4: $z^4=r^4e^{4i\theta}$.

misc.weak: $4\pi/3$ cannot represent the same direction as a principal argument.
misc.better: Subtract $2\pi$ to obtain the coterminal principal angle $-2\pi/3$.
The zero vector has no direction, so its argument is undefined.

misc.weak: Two sinusoidal waves with different frequencies can always be combined into one sinusoid by adding phasors.
misc.better: The single-phasor method here requires the same frequency.

terms.term: Write in polar or exponential form
terms.text: Give the modulus and an argument in the requested interval, using radians or degrees as specified.
Locate the point's quadrant, then express the angle in the specified principal interval.
Use the same frequency, combine coefficients and state the resulting amplitude and phase with an equivalent convention.

worked.prompt: Let $z=2e^{i\pi/3}$ and $w=3e^{-i\pi/4}$. Use radians and the principal argument interval $(-\pi,\pi]$ when requested.

parts.q: Write $z^4$ in exponential form using a principal argument.

kq.q: Why do complex numbers with arguments differing by $2\pi$ represent the same point?
kq.model: Sine and cosine are periodic with period $2\pi$, so both real and imaginary coordinates are unchanged.

kq.q: Why are moduli multiplied and arguments added in a product?
kq.model: Multiplying by a complex number applies its scaling and rotation. Two successive scalings multiply, while their rotation angles add.

kq.q: Why must the quadrant be checked when converting from Cartesian form?
kq.model: The tangent ratio alone does not distinguish all quadrants. The signs of the real and imaginary coordinates determine the correct direction.

kq.q: Why does the worked sinusoidal example have amplitude $\sqrt2$?
kq.model: After expansion the cosine and sine coefficients are 1 and $-1$. Their resultant amplitude is $\sqrt{1^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt2$.
